title: Excitation and the AVR: field current sets the voltage

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the voltage sagging under load and staying down with the AVR off, but coming back as the AVR raises the field up the open-circuit curve, when you drag the load up.
interactive.title: The AVR loop
interactive.whatAmILookingAt:
Twelve small screens on one picture, with Back and Continue. Five show an idea and seven ask you to try it. No marks and no timers.

The picture. At the top, a generator set is drawn side-on along one shaft, left to right. Each part has a one-word or two-word label. The PMG is a small permanent magnet generator. The exciter has its field ring fixed in the stator and its coils turning on the shaft. A diode bridge rides on the shaft. The main field sits on the rotor. The main stator's output leads run down to a load below. The labels read PMG, Exciter, Diodes, Main field, Stator and AVR. The AVR box sits off the shaft, with three leads. One brings its power in, from the PMG or from the output terminals. One senses the output. One feeds the exciter's fixed field. Two bars show the exciter's field current and the main field current. Each is a percentage of its value at no load and 440 V, so they move together. Below, the open-circuit curve plots the voltage the set makes inside, 0 to 600 V, against the field current, 0 to 200%. A dot sits at the present field current. A short line drops from the dot to the output voltage. That is the drop the load causes inside the machine. Beside it, a trace plots the output voltage against time, with the 440 V set point dashed. On a phone the curve and the trace stack. The load slider runs 0 to 100% of the set's rating in steps of 10, opening at 0%. The field-current slider runs 0 to 200% in steps of 5 and opens at 100%. It works only with the AVR off. An AVR switch turns it on and off. A supply switch, Shunt or PMG, lights where the AVR gets its power.

The readouts sit in three tiles: Load in %, Field current in % and Voltage in V. On a phone they wrap onto two rows. The two switches wrap too.

The rule it computes. The set is a 4-pole machine held at 1800 rev/min, so it makes 60 Hz throughout. Its field current is counted as a percentage of the field that makes 440 V with nothing connected. The curve is a sketch through these points: 0% gives 0 V, 25% gives 125 V, 50% gives 250 V, 75% gives 360 V, 100% gives 440 V, 125% gives 490 V, 150% gives 520 V, 175% gives 540 V and 200% gives 555 V. It runs straight between them. So it climbs steeply, then bends over at a knee where the iron saturates. The load drops 1 V inside the machine for each 1% of load, so 100 V at full load. So the output voltage = the curve's voltage at the present field − the load in %. With the AVR off, the field stays where the slider puts it. With the AVR on, it measures the output against its 440 V set point. It moves the field until they match. So it settles where the curve gives 440 V + the load in %. At 50% load that is 490 V, at 125%. At 100% load it is 540 V, at 175%. The main field is a large coil, so its current changes gradually. So a load step moves the output at once by the change in drop. The AVR then brings it back. That return is slowed so you can follow it. On Shunt, the AVR's supply bar follows the output voltage. On PMG it stays full. A short circuit on the board pulls the output to 0 V.

Screen 1, show. Nothing connected, the AVR off, the load slider hidden, the field-current slider free at 100%. The words: "This plot is the open-circuit curve. The set turns at a steady 1800 rev/min with nothing connected. So its voltage depends on the field current alone. Drag the field current up and watch the dot. At first the voltage climbs in step with the field. Then the curve bends over at a knee. There the iron saturates, as on a B-H curve. Past the knee, each extra step of field buys less voltage." Read: "The set turns at 1800 rev/min with nothing connected. Its voltage follows the field current along the open-circuit curve. It climbs in step at first. Then it bends over at a knee as the iron saturates." Still: nothing connected, the field at 200%, the dot at the top of the curve and the readouts at 0%, 200% and 555 V.

Screen 2, try it, typed. Nothing connected, the field at 100%. The Voltage tile reads ? until Check. "With nothing connected, the field current doubles from 100% to 200%. The curve marks 440 V at 100% and 555 V at 200%. How many times higher is the voltage now?" A field in ×. Answer 1.26 ×. Slips: 2 ×, "That holds only on the straight part. Past the knee the flux no longer keeps up with the field."; 0.79 ×, "That divides the wrong way round. The voltage went up." Hint when wrong: "Divide the new voltage by the old one." Why: "555 ÷ 440 = 1.26. The field current doubled, but the flux did not. The iron is saturating, so the voltage rose by only 26%." A right Check slides the field to 200% and the dot up the curve. Read: the question, word for word.

Screen 3, show. Nothing connected, the field at 100%, a Follow button lighting the current path from the AVR to the main field. The words: "The main field turns with the shaft. A brushless set has a second, smaller alternator on the same shaft. This is the exciter. Its field is fixed in the stator. Its coils turn on the shaft and make AC. A diode bridge on the shaft turns that AC into DC for the main field. The automatic voltage regulator, or AVR, feeds only the exciter's fixed field. The engine turning the shaft supplies the power. So a small current there controls a much bigger one in the main field." Read: "In a brushless set, the automatic voltage regulator, or AVR, feeds the exciter's fixed field. The exciter's turning coils make AC. A diode bridge on the shaft turns it into DC for the main field. No brushes are needed." Still: the whole path lit, from the AVR through the exciter and the diodes to the main field.

Screen 4, try it. "In a brushless set, which winding does the AVR's output feed?" Three choices, in this order, along the chain: "The exciter's fixed field"; "The main field on the rotor"; "The main stator's output coils". Right, the first. Hint for the second: "The main field turns with the shaft. The AVR sits still, so it reaches the main field only through the exciter and the diodes." Hint for the third: "Those coils carry the output. The AVR measures them, but it feeds a field." Why: "The AVR sits off the shaft. It feeds the exciter's fixed field, which needs no brushes. The exciter's turning coils and the diodes then carry a much bigger current into the main field." A right Check lights the AVR's lead to the exciter's field. Read: the question, word for word.

Screen 5, show. The AVR off, the field held at 100%, the load slider free from 0%. The words: "A load pulls the voltage down, and with the field held it stays down. The AVR is off and the field sits at 100%. Drag the load to 50%. The voltage falls from 440 V to 390 V and stays there. The load's current drops voltage inside the machine. A transformer's output falls on load in much the same way. Nothing has changed the field, so nothing brings the voltage back. Here the drop is drawn as 1 V for each 1% of load." Read: "The AVR is off and the field is held at 100%. The load's current drops voltage inside the machine. So a 50% load pulls the voltage down from 440 V to 390 V. It stays there." Still: the AVR off, the load at 50%, the trace stepping down to 390 V and running flat.

Screen 6, try it, typed. The AVR off, the field at 100%, the Voltage tile reading ? until Check. "The AVR is off and the field is held at 100%. The load goes from 0% to 80%. The drop is 1 V for each 1% of load. What voltage reaches the board?" A field in V. Answer 360 V. Slips: 440 V, "The field is held, but the load's current still drops voltage inside the machine."; 520 V, "The drop takes voltage away. It does not add it." Hint when wrong: "Work out the drop, then take it off 440 V." Why: "80% of load drops 80 V. The field has not moved, so the curve still gives 440 V inside. So 440 − 80 = 360 V reaches the board. It stays there." A right Check slides the load to 80%. Read: the question, word for word.

Screen 7, show. The AVR on, the load back at 0%, the load slider free. The words: "With the AVR on, the voltage comes back. Switch it on and drag the load to 50% again. The voltage dips towards 390 V at first. The main field is a big coil, so it cannot change in an instant. The AVR compares the output with its 440 V set point and raises the exciter's field. The load's drop is 50 V, so the set must make 490 V inside. The main field current climbs to 125%. The board gets 440 V again." Read: "With the AVR on, a 50% load dips the voltage towards 390 V at first. The AVR compares the output with its 440 V set point and raises the exciter's field. The load's drop is 50 V, so the set must make 490 V inside. The main field climbs to 125%, and the output returns to 440 V." Still: the AVR on, the load at 50%, settled, the trace showing the dip and the climb back.

Screen 8, try it, typed. The AVR on at 50% load, the Field current tile reading ? until Check. "The AVR holds 440 V at 50% load with the field at 125%. The load rises to 100%. The drop is 1 V for each 1% of load. The curve marks 490 V at 125%, 520 V at 150% and 540 V at 175%. What field current does the AVR settle at?" A field in %. Answer 175%. Slips: 150%, "That doubles the 25% the first half of the load took. Past the knee each step of field buys fewer volts."; 200%, "That adds 1% of field for each volt of drop. Read the curve instead."; 125%, "That leaves the field where it was. The AVR must make up the bigger drop." Hint when wrong: "Find the voltage the set must make inside, then read the curve." Why: "At 100% load the drop is 100 V. So the set must make 440 + 100 = 540 V inside. The curve gives 540 V at 175%. The first half of the load took 25% more field. The second half took 50%. The dot is now climbing past the knee." A right Check slides the load to 100% and lets the AVR settle. Read: the question, word for word.

Screen 9, show. The AVR on at 50% load, the supply switch free, opening on Shunt. The words: "The AVR needs power of its own. Flip the supply switch to see two common ways. On Shunt, it takes power from the set's own output. It needs no extra machine on the shaft. The set is then self-excited. On PMG, a permanent magnet generator on the same shaft feeds it. That power lasts as long as the shaft turns, whatever the output does. A self-excited set cannot keep up a short-circuit current. It dies away quickly unless the fault is cleared at once.[^1]" Read: "A shunt supply feeds the AVR from the set's own output. It needs no extra machine on the shaft. The set is then self-excited. A permanent magnet generator, or PMG, on the same shaft feeds it for as long as the shaft turns." Still: the AVR on at 50% load, the supply on Shunt, its path lit from the output terminals to the AVR.

Screen 10, try it. "A short circuit on the board pulls the set's output voltage close to zero. Which AVR supply can keep the field up?" Three choices, in this order: "Shunt, from the set's own output"; "PMG, on the same shaft"; "Either, since the shaft keeps turning". Right, the second. Hint for the first: "A shunt supply takes its power from the output. With the output near zero, the AVR has almost no power." Hint for the third: "The shaft turns either way. But only the PMG turns that into power for the AVR." Why: "The PMG takes its power from the shaft, not from the output. So the AVR can keep the exciter's field up through the fault. A shunt-fed AVR loses its power with the output. So the field and the fault current die away. The protection needs that current to last long enough to clear the fault." A right Check shorts the board: the load box reads Short in red, the output falls to 0 V and the Shunt power bar empties. Then the supply flips to PMG, its path lights and the bar fills. Read: the question, word for word.

Screen 11, try it, typed (mixed). The AVR on at 50% load, the Voltage tile reading ? until Check. "The AVR holds 440 V at 50% load, so the field sits at 125%. The load trips off. The curve marks 490 V at 125%. What is the voltage in the instant before the AVR acts?" A field in V. Answer 490 V. Slips: 440 V, "That is after the AVR has acted. The main field cannot change in an instant."; 390 V, "A trip takes the drop away, so the voltage jumps up." Hint when wrong: "Read the curve at the field the set has now. With no load, there is no drop to take off." Why: "The field is still at 125%, so the curve gives 490 V inside. With no load there is no drop. So the output jumps to 490 V. Then the AVR lowers the field until the board reads 440 V again." A right Check drops the load to 0% and plays the jump and the AVR's return. Read: the question, word for word.

Screen 12, try it, typed (mixed). The AVR on at 0% load, the Field current tile reading ? until Check. "The AVR is on and the load rises from 0% to 20%. The drop is 1 V for each 1% of load. The curve runs straight from 440 V at 100% to 490 V at 125%. What field current does the AVR settle at?" A field in %. Answer 110%. Slips: 120%, "That adds 1% of field for each volt. On this stretch 25% of field buys 50 V. So each volt needs 0.5%."; 100%, "That leaves the field where it was. The AVR must make up the 20 V drop." Hint when wrong: "Find the voltage inside first. Then see how far along the straight stretch it sits." Why: "The drop is 20 V, so the set must make 460 V inside. That is 20 V of the 50 V between 100% and 125%. So the field rises 20 ÷ 50 × 25 = 10%, to 110%." A right Check slides the load to 20%, and a closing line reads: "The field sets the voltage, and the AVR sets the field." Read: the question, word for word.
interactive.ignores: The curve is a sketch, run straight between its marked points. A real one is smooth and comes from the maker's test. The drop is drawn as a fixed 1 V for each 1% of load. A real drop does not grow in a straight line. It also depends on the kind of load. A lagging load drops more than a resistive one, and a leading load can raise the voltage instead. The speed is held steady, so the frequency never moves. A real load step also slows the engine for a moment. The AVR's return is slowed. It is drawn as a smooth climb with no overshoot. The main field is drawn in step with the exciter's field. A real exciter adds its own small delay and its own curve. The curve starts at 0 V. A real set still makes a small voltage with no field current, from the iron's leftover magnetism. Some sets feed the AVR from an extra winding in the main stator instead. The picture shows only Shunt and PMG.

explain.text:
The current in a generator set's turning field sets its voltage. A load drags that voltage down. So an [[automatic voltage regulator]], or AVR, measures the output and trims the field current to hold the voltage steady.

Run a set at its steady speed with nothing connected. Its voltage then depends on the field current alone, because the field current sets the flux. Plot one against the other and you get the [[open-circuit curve]]. It climbs in step at first. Then it bends over at a knee. There the iron saturates, as on a B-H curve. Past the knee, each extra step of field buys less voltage. On this sketch, doubling the field from 100% to 200% lifts 440 V only to 555 V.

Connect an ordinary load and the voltage falls. The load's current drops voltage inside the machine, much as a transformer's output falls on load. With the field held, the voltage stays down. So the field must rise as the load rises. The main field turns with the shaft. A brushless set feeds it with no sliding contact. A smaller alternator on the same shaft does the job. This is the [[exciter]]. Its field is fixed in the stator, and its coils turn on the shaft. A diode bridge riding on the shaft turns their AC into DC for the main field. The AVR feeds only the exciter's fixed field. The engine turning the shaft supplies the power. So a small current in the exciter's field steers a much bigger one in the main field.

The AVR works as a loop. It measures the output, compares it with its set point and corrects the field. Say the drop is 50 V at half load. The AVR raises the field until the curve gives 490 V inside, at 125%. Then 490 − 50 = 440 V reaches the board. At full load the drop is 100 V. The set must then make 540 V inside, which needs 175%. The second half of the load costs twice the field of the first, because of the knee. Bringing a set onto a live board and sharing load between sets build on this loop. They work by moving its set point, and the set point of the engine's speed control.[^4]

The AVR needs power too. A shunt supply takes it from the set's own output, so it needs no extra machine. The set is then self-excited. A permanent magnet generator, or PMG, on the same shaft gives power as long as the shaft turns. A self-excited set cannot keep up a short-circuit current. It dies away quickly unless the fault is cleared at once.[^1] That is a problem, because the protection needs time to clear the fault. An AVR supply of its own, such as a PMG, keeps the output up long enough.[^3] These numbers come from a simplified picture. Its curve is a sketch, and its drop grows in step with the load. A real drop depends on the kind of load. A leading load can even raise the voltage. **On a set running alone, the AVR holds the output voltage by adjusting the strength of the exciter's field.[^2] That field sets the main field current.**

analogy.text: Think of a battery charger on its constant-voltage stage. It measures the battery's voltage and compares it with its set voltage. Then it trims its output to hold that voltage. Put a load on the battery and the charger pushes more current. The AVR runs the same loop. It measures the output voltage and trims the field.
analogy.breaks: A charger trims its own output current directly. The AVR never touches the output current. It trims a small field two stages away, through the exciter and the diodes. The main field's coil makes it lag. And a charger has no knee. On the AVR's curve, past the knee, each extra step of field buys less voltage.

practice.text:
**Safety first:** treat a turning set as live, even with its breaker open and its AVR off. Its output, its exciter and its rotating diodes all carry voltage while the shaft turns. The iron's leftover magnetism makes some voltage even with no field current.

- Find out which supply feeds the AVR: shunt, PMG or a winding of its own. It tells you how the set behaves in a fault.
- On load, read the voltage together with the field current or the AVR's output. As the load rises, the field should rise and the voltage hold.
- If the voltage sags on load while the field stays put, the AVR is not correcting. Check its supply, its sensing lead and the exciter's field.
- If the field sits high on the curve at full load, the set is working past the knee. Each extra step of load then costs more field.

**Rule of thumb:** once the set works past the knee, each extra 1% of load costs more field than the last.

**Worked example:** take a set that makes 440 V with nothing connected at 100% field. Its drop is 1 V for each 1% of load, and its curve is the one drawn here. At 80% load the drop is 80 V. So the AVR must make 440 + 80 = 520 V inside. The curve gives 520 V at 150%, so the field settles at 150%. With the AVR off and the field left at 100%, the same load gives 440 − 80 = 360 V.

**Common mistakes**
- Expecting a set to hold its voltage by itself. With the field fixed, the voltage falls on load and stays down.
- Thinking the AVR of a brushless set drives the main field. It feeds the exciter's fixed field. The exciter and diodes then feed the main field.
- Expecting double the field to give double the voltage. Past the knee it gives much less.
- Expecting a self-excited set to keep feeding a short circuit. Its AVR loses its power with the output.
